                 COMMENTS OF PRIORITY POWER MANAGEMENT LLC
                        ON PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.521

     COMES NOW Priority Power Management LLC (PPM or Priority Power) and files these

comments regarding the Commission's proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC)

§ 25 . 521 , relating to Large Load Demand Management Service . This proposed rule is intended to

implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §39.170 as enacted by Senate Bill 6 (SB 6)

during the Texas Legislature's 89th Regular Session. The proposed rule would require ERCOT to

ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned

utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol to allow the transmission-

voltage customers to be curtailed during firm load shed; require ERCOT to develop a reliability

service to competitively procure demand reductions from large load customers; and establish a

framework for the program. The Commission has requested that comments be filed by September

4,2026, and therefore these comments are timely filed.

                                        INTRODUCTION

          PPM is a North America energy services firm that supports large commercial, industrial,

and public-sector customers with powered land development, private energy infrastructure

solutions, microgrid and behind-the-meter solutions, energy procurement, and ongoing market and

operational management. Priority Power delivers generation- and load-side solutions for

customers - including mission-critical facilities - to ensure reliable power and enable long-term

growth.
         PPM appreciates the opportunity to file comments on the Commission's proposed new

§ 25 . 521 , relating to Large Load Demand Management Service . The rule as proposed is a

reasonable implementation of the statute, and we have no specific proposed language changes at

this time. Below we respond to the four questions posed by the Commission in the preamble to the

proposed rule.

               COMMENTS ON QUESTIONS POSED BY THE COMMISSION

1. Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
   representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
   subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service
   (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not
   ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated
   some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer's availability to
   reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate
   payment to the large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation
   period?

        Yes, a large load customer that is available but not instructed to deploy during the LLDMS

obligation period should be compensated. Such customers will have taken actions to qualify for

and be available to deploy if instructed to do so. Loads offering this service are subject to testing

and may be penalized for non-performance, and therefore they should be paid for being ready to

perform accordingly. This approach is also consistent with ERCOT's existing treatment of Load

Resources providing ancillary services. Load Resources scheduled or selected in the Day-Ahead

Ancillary Service Market are eligible to receive a capacity payment regardless of whether they are

ultimately dispatched in Real-Time. 1 Similarly, LLDMS participants incur an obligation to remain

available to reduce demand during the obligation period, and that availability has value regardless

of whether ERCOT ultimately issues a deployment instruction.



1   Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT), Load Resource Participation in the El?COT Markets,
    https://www. ercot.com/services/programs/load/laar (last visited Sept. 4, 2026) (stating that Load Resources
    scheduled or selected in the ERCOT Day-Ahead Ancillary Service Market are eligible to receive a capacity
    payment regardless of whether dispatched in Real-Time).


                                     Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.521 - Page 2
        Paragraph (f)(1)(C) of the proposed rule specifies a payment of 25 percent of the market

clearing price (MCP). This payment is a reasonable starting point and can be evaluated over time

as experience is gained with the service.

2. Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar year.
   What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       It is not clear how the proposed $54 million annual budget was derived, and a transparent

basis for determining that figure would help the Commission determine whether that amount is

appropriate. The experience with Emergency Response Service (ER S) provides a useful

comparison. The Commission has adjusted the ERS expenditure limit over time, and ERCOT

currently publishes a methodology that allocates the ERS annual expenditure limit based on the

expected risk of deployment, considering factors including forecasted operating reserves,

forecasted load, and resource outages. PPM recommends that the budget be based on avoided cost

benefits related to averting an energy emergency alert (EEA-) load shed event. Further, the

methodology for establishing LLDMS budget should be transparent to market participants.

3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how far in
   advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

       PPM recommends that procurement be handled on an event-by-event basis. PURA §39.170

(b)(2) specifies that ERCOT must give large loads at least 24-hour notice for deployment.

Therefore, to allow preparation for deployment in a manner that accommodates the statutory

requirement for 24-hour notice, ERCOT should procure close to an anticipated procurement, but

no later than 48 hours before the anticipated deployment. Auction results should be posted on a

timely basis to allow market prices to be aligned with day ahead market clearing prices and other

ancillary service awards.




                                 Priority Power Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.521 - Page 3
 4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
   limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       Yes, ERCOT should be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies. PURA

§39.170(b) allows for"deployment in the event ofan anticipated emergency condition." Therefore,

such a broad scope would allow the LLDMS to be used for transmission emergencies as well as

other anticipated emergency conditions.

       This condition is not currently reflected in the rule as proposed. Subsection (e), which

governs deployment, is written entirely around weather-driven EEA events: subsection (e)(2)

authorizes deployment "during an EEA event due to an extreme weather condition," and subsection

(e)(3) ties the resumption obligation specifically to "the duration of the EEA event." If the

Commission extends deployment authority to transmission emergencies, PPM recommends that

subsection (e) also be revised to extend the same resumption obligation to that scenario.

                                          CONCLUSION

       PPM appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and respectfully requests that

the Commission adopt a rule consistent with these comments.

                                  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The rule as proposed is a reasonable implementation ofthe statute, and PPM has no specific

proposed language changes at this time. Responses to the four questions posed by the Commission

are as follows:

        1. Yes, a large load customer that is available but not instructed to deploy during the
           LLDMS obligation period should be compensated, as they have taken actions to be
           available to deploy. A payment of 25% of the MCP is reasonable.
       2. It is not clear how the $54 million was derived. PPM recommends that the budget be
          based on avoided cost benefits related to averting an EEA load shed event, and the
           methodology should be transparent.
       3. In order to allow preparation for a deployment in a manner that accommodates the
           statutory requirement for 24-hour notice, ERCOT should procure close to an
           anticipated procurement, but no later than 48 hours before the anticipated deployment.
       4. Yes, PURA §39.170(b) allows for "deployment in the event of an anticipated
          emergency condition." Therefore, such broad scope would allow the LLDMS to be
           used for transmission emergencies as well as other anticipated emergency conditions.
